drug_class: CD38-directed monoclonal antibody combined with an enzyme (hyaluronidase)
purpose: This medicine is used to treat multiple myeloma, which is a type of blood cancer that affects plasma cells in your bone marrow. It can be used alone or combined with other cancer medicines, depending on your situation. Your doctor will decide the best combination for you based on how far along your cancer is.
how_it_works: Think of this medicine as a smart guided missile. It contains a special protein called an antibody that recognizes and locks onto cancer cells by targeting a specific marker called CD38, which is found in large amounts on myeloma cancer cells. Once it attaches, it signals your immune system to attack and destroy those cancer cells. The hyaluronidase part is an enzyme that helps the medicine spread and absorb under your skin more easily so it can work faster.
common_side_effects: Common side effects include injection site reactions (redness, swelling, or pain where the shot is given), fatigue or feeling very tired, nausea, diarrhea, constipation, upper respiratory infections like a cold, muscle or back pain, and low blood cell counts which can increase your risk of infections or bleeding. Tell your doctor or nurse if any of these bother you.
warnings: This medicine can cause serious infusion or injection reactions, sometimes within 24 hours of getting the shot, so you will be watched closely and given pre-medications before each dose. It can lower your white blood cell count, making it harder for your body to fight infections, so avoid sick people and report any fever right away. It can interfere with certain blood type tests, so always tell any doctor or lab that you are taking this medicine. It may harm an unborn baby, so use reliable birth control during and for some time after treatment.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given as a shot just under the skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in your stomach area. It is typically given once a week at first, then every two weeks, and eventually once a month as your treatment progresses. Your cancer care team will set your exact schedule based on which treatment plan you are on. Each injection takes only about 3 to 5 minutes, which is much faster than the old IV version.
